question: Should I take lecture notes by hand or on a laptop? What does the research actually show?
verified: 2026-11-02. Every DOI, venue, year, volume and page below was read from Crossref and OpenAlex records; every finding and quote was read from the abstract named in abstract_source (OpenAlex, ERIC or Europe PMC). Sources marked abstract_source: null have no abstract in any open API, so only their metadata is recorded.

sources.authors: Mueller, P. A., & Oppenheimer, D. M.
sources.title: The pen is mightier than the keyboard: Advantages of longhand over laptop note taking
findings: In three studies, laptop note takers did worse than longhand note takers on conceptual questions.
Laptop note takers tended to transcribe lectures verbatim, which the authors argue is detrimental; taking more notes can help.
sources.quote: students who took notes on laptops performed worse on conceptual questions
sources.notes: Crossref lists a correction (corrigendum) published 2018-07-31, DOI 10.1177/0956797618781773. It is a correction, not a retraction.

sources.authors: Morehead, K., Dunlosky, J., & Rawson, K. A.
sources.title: How much mightier is the pen than the keyboard for note-taking? A replication and extension of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014)
sources.design: direct replication + extension (2 experiments) + meta-analysis of direct replications
sources.abstract_source: ERIC EJ1225471 (OpenAlex and Crossref have no abstract; the publisher withholds it)
findings: A direct replication (plus eWriter and no-notes groups) found some trends toward longhand, but performance did not consistently differ between groups.
Differences shrank further after students studied their notes.
Combining direct replications, longhand had small, nonsignificant advantages; the authors call choosing a winner premature.
sources.quote: performance did not consistently differ between any groups

sources.authors: Urry, H. L., et al. (88 authors)
sources.title: Don't ditch the laptop just yet: A direct replication of Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) Study 1 plus mini meta-analyses across similar studies
sources.design: direct replication (n = 74 laptop, 68 longhand) + mini meta-analyses of 8 studies
sources.abstract_source: OpenAlex (same text in Europe PMC, PMID 33539228)
findings: As in the original, laptop notes had more words and more verbatim overlap.
On the quiz, laptop users did no better than longhand users, and mini meta-analyses of eight similar studies pointed the same way.
Higher word count went with better quiz scores; the verbatim-overlap penalty was not robust.
Overall the results do not support the claim that longhand improves immediate learning via better encoding.
sources.quote: do not support the idea that longhand note taking improves immediate learning

sources.authors: Flanigan, A. E., Wheeler, J., Colliot, T., Lu, J., & Kiewra, K. A.
sources.title: Typed versus handwritten lecture notes and college student achievement: A meta-analysis
sources.abstract_source: ERIC EJ1430416 (OpenAlex and Crossref have no abstract)
findings: Across 24 studies, taking and reviewing handwritten notes was associated with higher achievement (Hedges' g = 0.248).
Typing produced much more note volume (Hedges' g = 0.919).
sources.quote: taking and reviewing handwritten notes leads to higher achievement

sources.authors: Voyer, D., Ronis, S. T., & Byers, N.
sources.title: The effect of notetaking method on academic performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.notes: Metadata verified (Crossref). No abstract in OpenAlex, Crossref, ERIC or Europe PMC, so its findings are not recorded here and a pipeline that only quotes abstracts cannot use it.

sources.authors: Luo, L., Kiewra, K. A., Flanigan, A. E., & Peteranetz, M. S.
sources.title: Laptop versus longhand note taking: Effects on lecture notes and achievement
sources.design: experiment (notes recorded vs recorded and reviewed)
findings: Laptop note takers recorded more notes and more verbatim lecture strings; longhand note takers recorded more visual notes.
Which medium helped depended on whether notes were only taken or also reviewed.
sources.quote: laptop note takers recorded more notes (idea units and words)

sources.authors: Bui, D. C., Myerson, J., & Hale, S.
sources.title: Note-taking with computers: Exploring alternative strategies for improved recall
findings: Transcribing on a computer gave the best immediate recall; organized notes did best on delayed tests, but with time to study, transcribers did better.
Note quantity predicted recall.
sources.quote: instructed to transcribe the lecture using a computer showed the best recall
sources.notes: OpenAlex lists the online year 2012; the issue (and Crossref) year is 2013.

sources.authors: Sana, F., Weston, T., & Cepeda, N. J.
sources.title: Laptop multitasking hinders classroom learning for both users and nearby peers
findings: Students who multitasked on a laptop during a lecture scored lower, and so did students who could see a multitasking peer.
sources.quote: participants who were in direct view of a multitasking peer scored lower

sources.authors: Ravizza, S. M., Uitvlugt, M. G., & Fenn, K. M.
sources.title: Logged in and zoned out: How laptop internet use relates to classroom learning
findings: Nonacademic internet use in class was common and inversely related to class performance, even after accounting for motivation, interest and intelligence.
Class-related internet use brought no benefit.
sources.quote: nonacademic Internet use was common among students who brought laptops to class

sources.title: In-class laptop use and its effects on student learning
sources.design: weekly surveys in a large lecture course (correlational)
findings: Students who used laptops in class multitasked a lot, and more laptop use went with lower scores on several measures of learning.
sources.quote: laptop use was negatively related to several measures of student learning

sources.authors: Carter, S. P., Greenberg, K., & Walker, M. S.
sources.title: The impact of computer usage on academic performance: Evidence from a randomized trial at the United States Military Academy
sources.notes: Metadata verified (Crossref). No abstract in any open API.

sources.authors: Van der Weel, F. R., & Van der Meer, A. L. H.
sources.title: Handwriting but not typewriting leads to widespread brain connectivity: A high-density EEG study with implications for the classroom
sources.design: EEG, 36 students writing visually presented words
findings: Handwriting words produced more elaborate brain connectivity patterns than typing them.
sources.quote: When writing by hand, brain connectivity patterns were far more elaborate
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed, but it measured brain activity while writing single words, not lecture note-taking or test scores. Use only with that caveat.

key_findings.finding: The famous 2014 study found longhand note takers did better on conceptual questions, linked to laptop users transcribing verbatim.
Direct replications (Morehead et al. 2019; Urry et al. 2021) found small, nonsignificant or no differences in test performance.
Syntheses: a 2024 meta-analysis found a small advantage for taking AND reviewing handwritten notes (g = 0.248); replication meta-analyses found small or no effects.
Typing produces more notes and more words, and more notes tend to go with better recall or quiz scores.
Whether students review or study their notes changes the picture (Flanigan 2024; Morehead 2019; Bui 2013; Luo 2018).
Off-task laptop use (multitasking, nonacademic internet) is linked to lower performance, including for nearby peers.

replication_nuance.rule: replications_smaller_or_none is covered AND the report cites the 2014 original

red_flags.rule: a cited work is retracted (OpenAlex is_retracted or a Crossref retraction/withdrawal notice)
red_flags.note: No source in this literature is retracted as of the verification date.

red_flags.rule: a cited DOI is neither in the run's fetched cache nor registered with the DOI system
a cited source is not a peer-reviewed journal article or review by the credibility rule (preprints, theses, datasets, news, blogs)
the report says the 2014 study was retracted (it has a 2018 correction, not a retraction)
the report overstates the evidence (e.g. 'proves', 'definitively', 'always better', 'far superior')
citing the 2024 EEG study as evidence that handwritten lecture notes raise grades (it measured brain connectivity while writing words)
citing the 2018 corrigendum as if it were a study
